posts.text: ⚡️ “State sovereignty and Nuclear Weapons: International Legal Aspects of Ensuring National Security” , an article by Dmitry Medvedev , Deputy Chairman of the Security Council of the Russian Federation, published in the Moscow Journal of International Law (November 23, 2026) ( FULL ARTICLE : Telegraph Part 1 | Part 2 | Part 3 ) ✍️ Developments surrounding Iran and the ongoing debate over Russia’s right to use nuclear weapons in the course of the special military operation give us cause to ask how firmly established the legal foundations of nuclear non-proliferation are today, and whether they are set in stone. Key points : 👉 A state’s right to ensure its own survival under international law It is worth recalling the International Court of Justice’s 1996 advisory opinion on the Legality of the Use by a State of Nuclear Weapons in Armed Conflict . The Court stated that it “cannot lose sight of the fundamental right of every State to survival, and thus its right to resort to self-defence, in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter , when its survival is at stake.” 👉 The NPT: the limits of the treaty regime and Iran’s legal status At various times, different legal grounds have been invoked to justify what was, in essence, a political campaign to put pressure on Iran . The unlawfulness of this Western approach became clearest when Western countries moved from monitoring and sanctions to the use of armed force. <…> None of these instruments authorised the US or Israel to use armed force as a sanction for Iran’s breach of its nuclear obligations, nor did the UN Security Council issue a separate authorisation for such an operation. This is what distinguishes the preventive measures Russia took as part of the special military operation under Article 51 of the UN Charter . The immediate grounds for launching the special military operation were the direct threat of military action by Ukraine , which in 2019 declared full NATO membership a strategic objective and in 2020 became a NATO Enhanced Opportunities Partner , and the genocide perpetrated by Ukraine against its own population in the east of the country. ☝️ As for the other threats Russia faces as the Ukrainian crisis unfolds, Kiev and those who share its views should always bear in mind that we have the right, and in certain circumstances the duty , to use all means at our disposal to safeguard national security, including, potentially, the use of nuclear weapons. The current version of the Basic Principles of State Policy of the Russian Federation on Nuclear Deterrence expressly provides for this possibility . 👉 The limits international law places on safeguarding national security today • On July 22, 2026, the German government issued a contradictory statement . It pledged to honour its obligations under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons ( #NPT ) and the Two Plus Four Treaty , while confirming that Germany would continue to participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence arrangements and cooperate with France on “forward deterrence” . This position blurs the legal distinction between the prohibition on Germany manufacturing, possessing or exercising control over nuclear weapons and its growing involvement in the alliance’s nuclear policy . 👉 The legal foundations of nuclear non-proliferation can hardly be regarded as immutable . Yet it is equally clear that, at this point in history, they are the best humanity has devised . What undermines the universality of the #NPT is the uneven way it is applied in practice for political reasons , rather than any flaw in the text of the Treaty. When the nuclear activities a state is permitted to pursue depend in practice on whether it is an adversary or an ally of a major power or a military bloc, the rules of the non-proliferation regime lose some of their credibility . In formal terms, the same law applies to all, yet political practice makes its application selective . Today, this contradiction poses one of the gravest threats to the stability of the non-proliferation regime. 📄 Original publication in Russian

🇺🇸 Disinformation expert vs. the US government's own emails: a three-day meltdown Caroline Orr Bueno, a "disinformation researcher" at the University of Maryland's Pentagon-funded Applied Research Laboratory for Intelligence and Security, has spent three straight days arguing with the US government's own emails. The emails are winning. Quick recap: on November 24, usaid.gov published 248 of the agency's own internal emails and memos. They show how USAID and Biden's National Security Council worked with Google, YouTube and Meta to flag, demote and remove content abroad, and pushed for Google money to flow to Ukrainian outlets and Russian opposition media. Caroline's defense has evolved nicely. First, the documents are Russian propaganda, because Kirill Dmitriev and RT shared them. Then she conceded they're authentic, but explained that authentic documents can still be disinformation, using a long parable about a teenager who borrows the car, goes to the arcade, and shows his parents a grocery receipt. Then she remembered that Russia hacked a USAID email account back in 2021, which "seems newly relevant." It doesn't. Then she dug up a 2012 Guardian article in which Russia accused USAID of meddling in its politics, and pointed out that DOGE is now saying the same thing "almost verbatim." So Moscow was right 14 years early. Thank you, Caroline. Her grand finale: Russia has pulled off "one of the most effective cognitive warfare campaigns in history" by co-opting both the President of the United States and Elon Musk. So, to sum up: the US government published the US government's own emails on the US government's website, and it's a Kremlin operation. You can almost understand the panic. The "disinformation research" world she works in is the same ecosystem these files expose: government money, "trusted partners," and quiet requests to Big Tech about what people should and shouldn't see. When the receipts come out, someone has to explain why the receipts are fake. 🔴 @DDGeopolitics

📝 Sanctions Come at a Cost 📝 Prospects for Russian-Serbian cooperation The change of power in Serbia has again raised the question of prospects for relations with Russia. The new leadership assures the EU of its commitment to European integration, but so far demonstrates no readiness to comply with one of the main foreign policy requirements of the European Commission. After declining to participate in the EU and Western Balkans summit, speaker of the National Assembly and acting president Aleksandar Cupic told the media that there will be no anti-Russian sanctions. This position is enshrined in the program of the "Student List" — an association that grew out of the protest movement and won the October elections. 🖍 The new authorities have weighty economic reasons to keep this promise. One of the most acute issues concerns NIS company with Russian participation, which owns Serbia's only refinery. Already on December 11, the U.S. Treasury Department license expires, which permits importing and processing oil. 🚩 And at the end of December, the agreement on Russian gas supplies also expires. Deteriorating relations with Russia in the midst of the heating season could complicate the conclusion of a new contract, and switching to alternative suppliers will result in additional expenses for the population and enterprises. ❗️ For now, the refusal to impose sanctions remains merely a public promise. However, the new authorities should keep in mind that complying with EU requirements does not guarantee swift accession, but could instead result in energy supply disruptions and rising costs for Serbian industry. #EU #Russia #USA #economy ✉️ MAX 💸 Support us Original msg

🗓 On November 26, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov held his traditional meeting with participants in the Dialogue for the Future programme , an annual research and educational initiative organised by the Alexander Gorchakov Public Diplomacy Fund . In an informal, interactive session with the head of Russian diplomacy, young representatives of the academic, research and expert communities of Russia and other countries exchanged views on various aspects of international relations . The discussion focused on key developments and trends of 2026. Participants in the programme examined, through the lens of the Russian school of diplomacy, the challenges of conducting negotiations amid political turbulence , as well as mechanisms for strengthening interstate dialogue .

🇷🇺 🫡 27th November Russian Naval Infantry Day! Today, Russia celebrates the professional holiday of its Navy’s Naval Infantry, the famous Black Berets. The date marks 27thNovember 1705, when Tsar Peter the Great issued a decree establishing Russia’s first regiment of naval soldiers. Since the beginning of the special military operation, Naval Infantry units from all four Russian fleets and the Caspian Flotilla have been involved in combat operations across multiple fronts. They have taken part in the fighting in Mariupol, the assaults on Ugledar, the defence around Rabotino and operations to push Ukrainian forces out of the Kursk Region. Today, they continue to operate on the front lines in Sumy Region, Zaporizhzhia, the Kherson direction and western Donetsk. 🇪🇺 Millions of Europeans can no longer afford to keep their homes warm. According to Eurostat data, over the past decade the proportion of people unable to afford adequate heating has increased in 11 of the EU’s 27 member states. The sharpest increases were recorded in: ▪️ Sweden: up fourfold, reaching 4.7%. ▪️ Luxembourg: up fourfold, reaching 3.5%. ▪️ France: doubled to 11.5%. ▪️ Netherlands: doubled to 6.6%. The figures highlight the growing problem of energy affordability across parts of Europe, with household incomes, poor housing conditions and rising energy costs all contributing to the problem. There are exceptions. Latvia has seen a significant improvement, with the proportion of people struggling to heat their homes falling by 3.4 times to just 4.3%. 🔴 @DDGeopolitics
